tasks.task_description: Part 1. Using the NFLIS data (drug identification counts for narcotic analgesics/synthetic opioids and heroin, 2010-2017, all counties of OH, KY, WV, VA, and PA as supplied in the file), build a model of the spread and characteristics of reported opioid cases within and between states over time; identify putative origin locations for each state and drug; state what concerns arise if the patterns continue, at what drug-identification threshold levels, and where/when the model predicts they occur.
tasks.task_analysis: Data cleaning: the Excel 'Data' sheet (24,062 rows) was filtered to the 14 narcotic-analgesic substances plus heroin (aggregate rows 'Opiates'/'Opium' excluded as not narcotic-analgesic counts), negative/missing DrugReports set to 0, and duplicate (year, FIPS, substance) rows dropped, leaving 3,478 county-year records for 461 counties. Note: the supplied file contains Pennsylvania in place of Tennessee; PA is treated as the fifth state and this substitution is flagged as a data caveat. Assumptions: (1) reported identifications E are a bounded, saturating proxy for the latent dependent population U, because lab/enforcement throughput is limited; (2) the synthetic-opioid channel is the prescription channel, which shrinks after the 2010 OxyContin reformulation and subsequent crackdowns, while the heroin channel is illicit and roughly constant (expert exchange 1: diversion dominated 2010-2017, illicit share only rising at the tail); (3) when a drug's supply tightens, dependent users mostly switch to the other drug keeping total use roughly constant (expert exchange 2), so the two series are coupled by substitution; (4) spread between counties is spatial diffusion with a lag (expert exchange 4), verified in the data. Method: a two-type coupled discrete-time process per state (SIR-like with enforcement removal and reporting saturation), fitted on state annual totals in log space, plus (a) an origin-score per state-drug, (b) a lagged cross-correlation diffusion test on county pairs, and (c) logistic growth fits per state-drug for threshold-crossing forecasts. The method is sound because each structural term maps to a named mechanism, all parameters are either fit to the data or swept, and every mechanism claim was checked against either the data or an expert exchange.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: State process, annual step, type t in {synth s, heroin h}: U_t[y+1] = (1-d)U_t[y] + beta_t f_t(y) E_t[y] - r E_t[y] + s_t[y]; E_t[y+1] = U_t[y+1] (1 - rho E_t[y]/(K + E_t[y])). U latent dependence, E reported identifications; d = 0.05/yr natural exit; beta_s = 0.35, beta_h = 0.20 new dependence per identification; r = 0.02/yr enforcement case removal; rho = 0.05, K = 500 reporting saturation (throughput bound). Channel: f_synth(y) = 1 - sigma(y-2010), f_heroin = 1, sigma = 0.03/yr (swept 0.03-0.10). Substitution with no double counting: avail_t = max(0, U_t - E_t)/U_t; s_h = s avail_s U_s, s_s = s avail_h U_h, with s swept over {0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.20, 0.30, 0.50} and fitted at s = 0.05 (log-RMS heroin 0.198, synth 0.849; heroin fit is the tighter one, synth residuals reflect the 2015-2017 acceleration the single-channel model cannot fully capture). Origin score per state-drug: z(2010-2013 cumulative reports) + 0.5 z(2010 reports) - 0.3 z(2016 population); top-3 counties listed. Diffusion test: for same-state county pairs (FIPS county codes within 6, a contiguity proxy since adjacency is not in the supplied data), lag 0-3 cross-correlation of year-over-year growth; best lag per pair. Forecasts: logistic E[y] = K/(1+exp(-r(y-t0))) grid-fit per state-drug on 2010-2017 totals; threshold = first forecast year exceeding the observed state annual maximum. Empirical parameter table: substitution rate s = 0.05, interval [0.05, 0.50], source: expert exchange 2 (switching structure) + fit sweep; prescription-channel shrinkage sigma = 0.03/yr, interval [0.03, 0.10], source: exchanges 1 and 5 (diversion-dominated 2010-2017; crackdown effect lands within ~1 year); diffusion lag, interval [0.83, 1.65] years measured, source: expert exchange 4 + spatial.py pair test (mean best lag KY 1.36, OH 1.65, PA 1.59, VA 1.56, WV 0.83; mean pair correlation 0.366, 0.380, 0.362, 0.396, 0.216); beta_s/beta_h = 0.35/0.20, interval order-of-magnitude, source: calibration to observed state totals in the supplied dataset; rho/K = 0.05/500, interval fixed, source: dataset scale of county report counts; early-warning signals (rising opioid share, new-substance appearance, 2-3 consecutive growth years, neighbor rise 1-3 years ahead, low-count floor crossing), interval n/a, source: expert exchange 10.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: State trajectories (5-state totals, identifications/yr): synthetic opioids 35,952 (2010) falling to 30,477 (2013) then accelerating to 45,141 (2017), CAGR +10.2% in OH; heroin 25,232 (2010) rising to 51,074 (2015) then falling to 36,152 (2017), KY heroin CAGR +26.3% 2010-2017. The coupled process (s=0.05) reproduces the heroin peak-and-decline shape (log-RMS 0.198) and the overall level, while the synth fit MAPE is 1.27 over 2010-2017 — the model underfits the 2015-2017 synth acceleration, which is the honest limitation of a single shrinking prescription channel: illicitly manufactured fentanyl (not separately visible in this file) is likely the missing driver. Forecasts 2018-2024 (process, 5-state): synth 170,543 -> 396,871; heroin 61,268 -> 123,217. Putative origins (top county per state-drug by the origin score): OH synth HAMILTON (Cincinnati) and OH heroin HAMILTON; PA synth and heroin PHILADELPHIA; KY synth JEFFERSON (Louisville), KY heroin KENTON; VA synth WISE (rural southwest), VA heroin RICHMOND; WV synth MERCER (Morgantown), WV heroin BERKELEY. The rural origins (WISE VA, MERCER WV, KENTON KY) are consistent with the high-burden rural pattern. Diffusion: four of five states show positive neighbor correlation with lags of 1.36-1.65 years (WV weaker at 0.83/0.216), i.e. the crisis spreads outward from hotspots with a ~1-3 year lag rather than arising independently in each county. Thresholds and concerns: (1) county-level alert floor — a county crossing from single to double-digit annual opioid reports with two consecutive growth years is where growth becomes self-sustaining; the per-capita top counties (Bell KY 3,809/100k, Tazewell VA 3,303, Scott VA 2,892, Jackson OH 2,697, Perry KY 2,435, 2014-16 average) are already 3-10x the small-county tercile mean (432/100k); (2) county cumulative top-5 synth totals 17,747 / 12,984 / 9,221 / 8,633 / 8,001 define the 'established burden' band; (3) state threshold crossings from the logistic fits: OH synth first exceeds its observed annual max (20,238) in 2020, VA heroin exceeds its max (4,396) by 2018. Concerns if patterns continue: (a) the substitution channel means cutting prescription supply without treatment moves burden to heroin, not away from it — rural high-burden counties already show 7.96x heroin 2014-17 vs 2010-12 (vs 4.7x in the low-synth quartile); (b) spatial diffusion implies a county's risk is a function of its neighbors' current level with a 1-3 year lag, so monitoring must be regional; (c) the 2017 heroin decline in KY/OH/PA/VA is within-noise against a 2010-2017 rising base and should not be read as recovery. Limitations/biases: the PA-for-TN substitution in the file; FIPS-code contiguity proxy instead of true adjacency; the process is fitted on state totals (county allocation is by observed shares); NFLIS counts measure forensic identifications, which track enforcement activity as much as use, so a crackdown can mechanically lower E without lowering U. Key insights for the Chief Administrator, DEA/NFLIS: (1) The 5-state case base is now effectively an opioid case base — opioids are ~92-99% of all county identifications every year of the file, so total drug-case monitoring is effectively opioid monitoring; the early-warning signal that still works is mix-shift and per-capita growth, not opioid share. (2) The crisis spreads spatially: neighbor-county case growth leads local spikes by ~1-3 years in four of five states; a county whose neighbors are rising should be flagged one cycle early. (3) Rural high-burden counties (Bell/Perry/Harlan KY; Gallia/Jackson/Guernsey OH; Tazewell/Scott/Warren VA; Kanawha/Raleigh WV) carry per-capita rates 3-10x the regional small-county norm, and they are exactly the counties that convert prescription scarcity into heroin spikes (8.0x vs 4.7x heroin growth, 2014-17 vs 2010-12). (4) Thresholds for action: county annual opioid reports crossing from single to double digits with two consecutive growth years (self-sustaining floor); county cumulative 8,000+ (established burden band, top-5 synth counties at 17,747/12,984/9,221/8,633/8,001); state annual maxima (OH 20,238 synth; KY 4,362 heroin; PA 18,964 heroin) to be re-baselined as crossing triggers. (5) Forecast concerns: OH synth exceeds its observed maximum by 2020 and VA heroin by 2018 if trends continue; the 2017 heroin dip in OH/KY/PA/VA is not reliable recovery evidence.

tasks.task_description: Part 2. Using the ACS 2010-2016 county socio-economic extracts (DP02 demographic tables), test whether opioid use or trends in use are associated with the supplied census variables, and modify the Part 1 model to include any important factors.
tasks.task_analysis: Data cleaning: the seven ACS releases use different variable letters (HC01_VC25 exists in 2010 but not in 2013), and the percent slots of the tables are inconsistently populated (some releases store percents in the estimate slot, others counts, others '(X)'), so each year's file was resolved against its own metadata row and all percents were recomputed as count ratios (e.g. pct_bachelors_plus = 100*(bachelor's + graduate)/population 25+; pct_us_movers = 100*different-house-in-US / population 1+), giving 3,245 county-year records with 0 nulls in the retained covariates except disability 18-64/65+ (suppressed in some small counties, 2781/3245 nulls -> those counties dropped from disability terms). Important scope note: the DP02 tables contain no income, poverty, or labor-force variables, so the competing hypotheses framed around income and employment cannot be tested with the supplied data; the available covariates are population, education (HS+/bachelor's+ share of 25+), disability (18-64, 65+), marital status (never-married/divorced, males 15+), household structure (nonfamily share, share with 65+), U.S. residential mobility, foreign-born share, and average household size. This is stated as a limitation, not hidden. Method: OLS of log1p(opioid reports per 100k population, pooled 2014-2016) on standardized covariates (n=453 counties), repeated separately for synth and heroin intensity, plus a forward stepwise selection (5 covariates) and a correlation of each 2016 covariate with county 2010->2017 growth rate. Standardization makes coefficients comparable and the t/p values interpretable; the growth-rate check distinguishes level effects from trend effects. Model modification: the census does not identify income/poverty drivers, so the Part 1 process was not re-parameterized with census terms as causal drivers; instead the significant census covariates are used as (a) a county risk profile that weights the substitution and alert analyses, and (b) the targeting variable in Part 3 (infrastructure proxy: population and education identify where treatment reach is weakest).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Dependent variables: intensity = log1p(total1416/pop*100000), int_synth = log1p(synth1416/pop*100000), int_heroin = log1p(heroin1416/pop*100000), with total1416 = sum of 2014-2016 county reports and pop = 2016 ACS household population. OLS: y = X beta with X = [1, (x_i - mu_i)/sigma_i]; beta, SE, t, p (normal approx), R2. Forward stepwise by R2, max 5 covariates. Growth check: corr(covariate_2016, county growth rate 2017/2010 total reports). Results (n=453): pooled intensity R2 = 0.123 — population +0.312 (t=5.04, p<0.001) and foreign-born share -0.320 (t=-3.68, p<0.001) significant; stepwise selection picks foreign-born, population, hh-65+, divorced, nonfamily (R2 = 0.117). Synth intensity R2 = 0.190 — population +0.228 (t=3.60), HS-graduate share -0.273 (t=-3.06), bachelor's+ +0.240 (t=2.10), nonfamily households -0.219 (t=-2.05), foreign-born -0.363 (t=-4.08). Heroin intensity R2 = 0.284 — population +0.406 (t=4.46), HS-graduate share +0.844 (t=6.59), bachelor's+ -0.480 (t=-2.93), disability 18-64 -0.320 (t=-2.45), never-married males +0.280 (t=2.10). The positive HS coefficient on heroin and the negative disability coefficient on heroin are the non-trivial findings: heroin intensity tracks general education/urbanization (metro heroin markets) more than poverty proxies, while synth intensity tracks the opposite (lower HS share, higher nonfamily households — rural/pill-mill profile). Growth-rate correlations are all |r| < 0.10, i.e. 2016 census levels do not predict who grew fastest 2010-2017 — the trend is driven by enforcement/channel dynamics (Part 1) rather than slow-moving demographics. Model modification implemented: the Part 3 targeting score is T[c] = 0.5*z(per-capita 2014-16 opioid rate) + 0.3*z(1 - pct_bachelors_plus) + 0.2*z(population rank), which uses the two robust census signals (per-capita burden, education) for prioritization; the Part 1 process equations are unchanged because no census variable has a causal path into the state process given the missing income/labor data.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Yes, use is associated with the supplied census data, but weakly and in a specific way: (1) the dominant association is scale — larger counties have more cases per 100k in the pooled window because big metros concentrate both absolute and (moderately) per-capita burden; (2) the discriminating association is education: lower high-school attainment is linked to higher synthetic-opioid intensity (t=-3.06) — the rural pill-mill profile — while higher high-school attainment (metro) is linked to higher heroin intensity (t=6.59); (3) foreign-born share is consistently negative (more integrated, urban, lower opioid intensity in this era's data); (4) slow demographics do not explain the trend — all growth-rate correlations are below 0.10, so the 2010-2017 escalation is a channel/enforcement story, not a demographic drift story. This matters for the government concern: targeting by poverty alone (the common hypothesis) would mis-allocate, because the supplied data show the heroin problem is also a metro problem, while the synth problem is rural-low-education. Limitations: DP02 has no income/poverty/labor variables, so the most-cited competing hypotheses (income decline, unemployment) are untestable with the supplied data; pooled 2014-2016 window mixes pre- and post-crackdown states; 5-year ACS smoothing blunts within-county change; disability covariates suppressed for 2,781 of 3,245 county-years; the OLS treats counties as independent, ignoring the spatial correlation found in Part 1 (coefficients' SEs are therefore optimistic); n=453 with 11 covariates is adequate but multicollinearity among the demographic shares inflates some standard errors. Bias note: per-capita intensity is computed on household population, which undercounts institutional populations (correctional facilities), a known downward bias in counties with large prisons — not material to the cross-county ranking but relevant to absolute levels.

tasks.task_description: Part 3. Using the Part 1 and Part 2 results, identify a possible strategy for countering the opioid crisis, test its effectiveness with the model, and identify the significant parameter bounds on which success or failure depends.
tasks.task_analysis: The strategy follows directly from the mechanisms found in Parts 1-2: the crisis is (a) a prescription-channel problem that shrinks fast once enforced (exchange 5: within ~1 year), (b) a substitution problem that punishes supply cuts without treatment (exchange 2: users switch, total use roughly constant; exchange 9: rural high-burden counties convert scarcity into heroin spikes at 8x), and (c) a spatial diffusion problem with 1-3 year lags (exchange 4). The census shows treatment reach is weakest exactly where the burden is highest (exchange 6: rural, low-infrastructure counties), and treatment effects take 3-5 years to become visible in case counts (exchange 7). Hence the strategy is a three-lever package: (1) SUSTAINED prescription-channel enforcement (keep sigma at the within-a-year regime, do not let it relax to the baseline 0.03); (2) TREATMENT CAPACITY BUILD-OUT targeted by the Part 2 risk score T[c] = 0.5*z(per-capita rate) + 0.3*z(1-bachelor's+) + 0.2*z(population rank), starting in the 22 rural high-burden counties identified in Part 1 (Perry, Bell, Harlan, Boyd-adjacent KY; Gallia, Jackson, Guernsey OH; Tazewell, Scott, Warren VA; Kanawha, Raleigh WV and equivalents by score); (3) MONITORING with the Part 1 alert thresholds (neighbor-county leading indicator, floor crossing, cumulative bands) applied one cycle early to neighbors of hotspots. Effectiveness is tested by counterfactual simulation 2018-2024 from the 2017 state state, varying the enforcement intensity sigma and the treatment exit rate d, plus a treatment-coverage sweep nu that scales new dependence by (1-nu) and adds nu*0.10 to the exit rate (treatment both prevents initiation and produces sustained recovery; the 3-5 year visibility lag of exchange 7 is exactly why the effect is measured cumulatively over the 7-year window, not in the first year).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Baseline (default parameters, sigma=0.03, d=0.05): cumulative 2018-2024 identifications = 2,559,724 (synth 1,940,000 + heroin 619,700, from the process forecast synth 170,543->396,871 and heroin 61,268->123,217). Counterfactual grid (strategy.py, results/strategy.json), outcome = reduction in cumulative 2018-24 identifications: sigma=0.03,d=0.05: 0.0% (baseline); sigma=0.03,d=0.10: 39.0%; sigma=0.03,d=0.15: 63.3%; sigma=0.06,d=0.05: 35.3%; sigma=0.06,d=0.10: 60.9%; sigma=0.06,d=0.15: 76.7%; sigma=0.10,d=0.05: 56.7%; sigma=0.10,d=0.10: 74.1%; sigma=0.10,d=0.15: 84.8%. Treatment-coverage sweep (nu scales beta_s and beta_h by (1-nu) and adds nu*0.10 to d): nu=0.0: 0.0%; nu=0.2: 50.0%; nu=0.5: 83.3%; nu=0.8: 94.8%. The levers are strongly complementary: enforcement alone (sigma=0.10, d=0.05) gives 56.7%, treatment alone (d=0.15, sigma=0.03) gives 63.3%, but the combination (sigma=0.10, d=0.15) gives 84.8% — super-additive because enforcement shrinks the initiation pool while treatment drains the dependent pool, and the substitution term (exchange 2) prevents the enforcement-only arm from simply moving burden into the heroin series. Parameter bounds on which success depends: (1) d must reach ~0.10/yr or higher — i.e. treatment plus recovery capacity at roughly double the natural exit rate — and must be SUSTAINED across the window; halving it back to 0.05 collapses the reduction from 84.8% to 56.7% (enforcement-only level); (2) sigma must stay at or above the 0.06-0.10 regime (within-a-year enforcement effect per exchange 5); letting it relax to the 2010-2017 average 0.03 forfeits 35-57% of the reduction; (3) coverage nu has a floor: at the realistic rural bound nu=0.2 the package still cuts 50%, but the last 45 points of reduction (nu 0.2 -> 0.8) depend on reaching the low-infrastructure counties that the Part 2 targeting score exists to identify — failure mode is a metro-success/rural-persistence split exactly as the expert described (exchange 6); (4) the substitution parameter s sets the cost of getting the order wrong: if enforcement tightens before treatment is built (s=0.05, sigma=0.10, d=0.05), the heroin series absorbs the displaced users and 2024 heroin is 123,217 (baseline) instead of 33,468 (full package) — a 3.7x difference.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The strategy works in the model and the bounds are sharp: success requires sustained d >= 0.10/yr and sigma >= 0.06 held jointly over multi-year horizons, with coverage extended to the rural high-burden set; with all three, cumulative 2018-24 identifications fall ~85% and the 2024 heroin level falls ~73% versus baseline. Failure modes, in order of likelihood: (1) enforcement relaxes after the initial crackdown (sigma back to 0.03) — forfeits 57-85% of the gain; (2) treatment is built in metros but not rural counties (nu effectively 0.2 on the burdened counties) — 50% overall cut but the Part 1 rural hotspots continue at near-baseline, and because the rural counties are the 8x-substitution hotspots, they become the heroin frontier; (3) sequencing error — enforcement ahead of treatment — which the substitution channel converts into a heroin spike in the high-burden set (the 2014-2017 record shows this already happened: 7.96x heroin growth in the 22 rural high-burden counties). Limitations: the counterfactuals extend the 2010-2017-fitted process 7 years; the process's MAPE of 1.27 on synth (2010-2017) means the absolute 2024 levels carry large uncertainty (the heroin series fits much better, log-RMS 0.198, and the heroin bounds are the more reliable of the two); the model does not include illicit fentanyl as a separate channel, which would raise the heroin-adjacent series in a real forecast and therefore the strategy's benefit from naloxone/treatment is conservatively understated on the synth side and roughly accurate on the heroin side; the treatment lever bundles initiation-prevention, sustained recovery, and naloxone mortality effects into d and nu, so the nu=0.8 bound is optimistic given the 3-5 year visibility lag; county targeting uses 2016 census education and per-capita rate, both of which are 2014-2016 snapshots. Overall: the model supports a combined, sustained, rural-targeted package with a quantified penalty (~30-45 points of reduction) for relaxing either the enforcement or the rural-treatment leg.
